'''Diana Valencia''' (born 1978) is a Colombian [[planetary scientist]] and [[astrophysics|astrophysicist]]. She is an associate professor of Physics and Astrophysics, [[University of Toronto Scarborough]], and of [[Astronomy]] & Astrophysics, [[University of Toronto Faculty of Arts and Science]].<ref name="El_Espectador">{{cite news |last1=Monsalve |first1=Maria Mónica |title=Tres astrónomas colombianas que la están rompiendo |url=https://www.elespectador.com/noticias/ciencia/tres-astronomas-colombianas-que-la-estan-rompiendo-articulo-838947 |accessdate=24 November 2019 |work=El Espectador |issue=Ciencia |publisher=El Espectador |location=Bogota, Colombia |language=Spanish |date=10 February 2019 |ref=Articulo-838947}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Valencia |first1=Diana |title=Dr. |url=https://www.utsc.utoronto.ca/physsci/diana-valencia |website=University of Toronto Scarborough Faculty |publisher=University of Toronto Scarborough |accessdate=20 November 2019}}</ref>

Valencia’s research characterizes planets with masses between [[gas giants]] and Earth’s.<ref name="First Super-Earth Article">{{cite journal |last1=Valencia |first1=Diana |last2=Sasselov |first2=Dimitar D. |last3=O'Connell |first3=Richard J. |title=Radius and Structure Models of the First Super-Earth Planet |journal=The Astrophysical Journal |date=10 February 2007 |volume=656 |issue=1 |pages=545–551 |doi=10.1086/509800 |bibcode=2007ApJ...656..545V |arxiv=astro-ph/0610122 |s2cid=17656317 }}</ref>

==Biography==

Diana Valencia immigrated from Colombia to [[Canada]] with her parents when she was studying a B.S. in Physics from [[University of Los Andes (Colombia)|University of Los Andes]], Colombia. Though from a family of engineers, she intended to become a historian or economist in Colombia. Ultimately, she was influenced by her chemical engineer mother, despite her mother's misogynistic experiences in Colombia.<ref name="HoraPico">{{cite web |last1=Salazar |first1=Isabel |last2=Montoya |first2=Carolina |title=Entrevista a Diana Valencia, astrofísica planetaria |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fQZ2-Bv3A98&feature=youtu.be |website=HoraPico |publisher=Republic of Colombia |accessdate=23 November 2019 |location=Bogota, Colombia |language=Spanish |format=Live Television Interview |date=19 February 2019}}</ref>  Once in Canada, she realized there were career opportunities for women in the sciences and earned a B.A., then M.S. in Physics at University of Toronto. Valencia was inspired to apply for post-graduate programs and was accepted into Harvard University as a doctoral student.<ref name="El_Espectador" /><ref name="Univ of Toronto CV">{{cite web |last1=Valencia |first1=Diana |title=Curriculum Vitae |url=http://astro.utoronto.ca/~valencia/curriculum/cv.html |website=University of Toronto Department of Astronomy & Astrophysics Directory Website |publisher=University of Toronto |accessdate=21 November 2019}}</ref>

==Selected academic work==

In 2006, Valencia's first major publication, "Internal Structure of Massive Terrestrial Planets", proposed the first mass-radius relationship for rocky exoplanets that associated mass, radius, and internal structure of solid planets more massive than Earth.<ref name="Internal Structure of Massive Terrestrial Planets">{{cite journal |last1=Valencia |first1=Diana |last2=O'Connell |first2=Richard J. |last3=Sasselov |first3=Dimitar |title=Internal Structure of Massive Terrestrial Planets |journal=Icarus |date=April 2006 |volume=181 |issue=2 |pages=545–554 |doi=10.1016/j.icarus.2005.11.021 |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/journal/icarus/vol/181/issue/2 |accessdate=22 November 2019|bibcode=2006Icar..181..545V |arxiv=astro-ph/0511150 |s2cid=118946944 }}</ref>

2007's publication, "Radius and Structure Models of the First Super-Earth Planet", recognized that exoplanets of different compositions would have different mass and radius measurements as quantified by degeneracy pressures, including exoplanets with iron cores, rocky mantles, and icy/liquid shells.<ref name="Internal Structure of Massive Terrestrial Planets" />

Recognizing that human interest in the habitability of extra-solar planets drives much of their investigation, and that plate tectonics plays an important role in life on Earth, another 2007 publication, "Inevitability of Plate Tectonics on Super-Earths", was the first published investigation to propose that larger-massed terrestrial planets should experience plate tectonics due to thinner, weaker lithospheres and higher stresses.<ref name="Inevitability">{{cite journal |last1=Valencia |first1=Diana |last2=O'Connell |first2=Richard J. |last3=Sasselov |first3=Dimitar D. |title=Inevitability of Plate Tectonics on Super-Earths |journal=The Astrophysical Journal Letters |date=20 November 2007 |volume=670 |issue=1 |pages=45–48 |doi=10.1086/524012 |bibcode=2007ApJ...670L..45V |arxiv=0710.0699 |s2cid=9432267 }}</ref>

In 2013, "Bulk Composition of GJ 1214b and Other Sub-Neptunian Exoplanets", attempts to show an atmospheric exoplanet's composition was attained based on planetary mass and radius, and its evolution and internal characteristics.<ref name="Bulk Composition Sub-Neptunian">{{cite journal |last1=Valencia |first1=Diana |last2=Guillot |first2=Tristan |last3=Parmentier |first3=Vivien |last4=Freedman |first4=Richard S. |title=BULK COMPOSITION OF GJ 1214b AND OTHER SUB-NEPTUNE EXOPLANETS |journal=The Astrophysical Journal |date=29 August 2013 |volume=775 |issue=1 |pages=10 |doi=10.1088/0004-637X/775/1/10 |bibcode=2013ApJ...775...10V |arxiv=1305.2629 |s2cid=73684175 }}</ref>

2018’s "Habitability from Tidally Induced Tectonics" introduced the mechanism of vertical recycling of carbon through a planet's volcanic activity and sequestered carbon onto, and with, the basaltic oceanic crust settling ("foundering") and re-entering the mantle. This heat-pipe tectonism is equivalent to Earth's plate tectonics, enabling carbon-silicate cycling, thereby maintaining Earth habitable for billions of years.<ref name="Habitability from Tidal Tectonics">{{cite journal |last1=Valencia |first1=Diana |last2=Tan |first2=Vivian Yun Yan |last3=Zajac |first3=Zachary |date=20 April 2018 |title=Habitability from Tidally Induced Tectonics |journal=The Astrophysical Journal |volume=857 |issue=2 |pages=106 |arxiv=1803.07040 |bibcode=2018ApJ...857..106V |doi=10.3847/1538-4357/aab767|s2cid=73541914 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

"Can a Machine Learn the Outcome of Planetary Collisions?", published 2019, explores improved methods of predicting the outcome of planetary collisions thought to be important in the last stages of planet formation. This machine learning approach seems a promising avenue. The methodology identifies variables needing further investigation to build better predictive models as large ratio of target to impactor masses and low velocities.<ref name="Machine Learned Collisions">{{cite journal |last1=Valencia |first1=Diana |last2=Paracha |first2=Emaad |last3=Jackson |first3=Alan P. |title=Can a Machine Learn the Outcome of Planetary Collisions? |journal=The Astrophysical Journal |date=29 August 2019 |volume=882 |issue=1 |pages=35 |doi=10.3847/1538-4357/ab2bfb |bibcode=2019ApJ...882...35V |arxiv=1902.04052 |s2cid=119390146 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

==Recognition==

* 2008 Poincaré Postdoctoral Fellowship at Observatoire de la Côte d'Azur, Nice, France<ref name="Sagan Fellowship">{{cite web |title=Sagan Postdoctoral Fellowship Recipients 2010 Postdoctoral Fellows |url=http://nexsci.caltech.edu/sagan/2010postdocRecipients.shtml |website=Sagan Postdoctoral Fellowship Recipients 2010 Postdoctoral Fellows |publisher=California Institute of Technology, National Aeronautics and Space Administration |accessdate=25 November 2019}}</ref>
* Alumna of the Origins of Life Institute, department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, Harvard University<ref name="Origins of Life">{{cite web |title=Origins of Life Initiative |url=https://origins.harvard.edu/people/role/alumni?page=3 |website=Origins of Life Initiative |publisher=The President and Fellows of Harvard College |accessdate=25 November 2019}}</ref>
* 2010 Sagan NASA Postdoctoral Fellow<ref name="Sagan Fellowship" />
* 2021 International Paolo Farinella Prize, awarded by the European Planetary Society for her significant contributions in our understanding of the interior structure and dynamics of terrestrial and super-Earth exoplanets. This prize was shared with Lena Noack.
